cards.title: Why DHCP
cards.body: DHCP hands a host all four settings automatically. Addresses are leased for a set time, so the server can reuse those of devices that leave. No typing mistakes, and a laptop can join any network.

visual.caption: DHCP runs over UDP: servers listen on port 67, clients on 68

cards.title: The DORA exchange
cards.body: Four messages, remembered as DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

frames.caption: Discover: the client broadcasts, looking for any server
Offer: a server offers an address and settings
Request: the client asks for the offered address
Acknowledge: the server confirms and the lease starts

cards.title: No address yet
cards.body: While it asks, the client has no IP address. Its broadcast reaches every host on this LAN only: routers never forward it. Replies may be broadcast too; the client spots its own by the client ID inside.

visual.caption: From nobody (0.0.0.0) to everybody on the LAN

cards.title: DHCP relay
cards.body: A central server can't hear broadcasts from other subnets. So the router on each LAN acts as a relay agent (on Cisco, the ip helper-address command).

frames.caption: The PC broadcasts a Discover; it stops at the LAN router
The relay forwards it as a unicast to the server's address
The server answers the relay, also by unicast
The relay passes the reply back onto the LAN

cards.title: Leases and renewal
cards.body: The server keeps an address pool per subnet, skips excluded addresses kept for static use, and sets the lease time. By default the client renews with its own server at 50% (T1) and asks any server at 87.5% (T2).

events.what: T1, halfway: ask the same server to renew
T2, 87.5%: still no answer, so ask any server
The lease runs out if nobody renewed it

visual.caption: Half of 24 hours after 06:00 is 18:00

cards.title: When DHCP fails
cards.body: A 169.254.x.x address (from 169.254.0.0/16) means: check the path to the DHCP server.

visual.caption: Link-local (APIPA): only other 169.254 hosts on the link are reachable

cards.title: Names to numbers
cards.body: People type names; packets need IP addresses. A host asks the DNS server it learned from DHCP or its settings. Queries use port 53, usually over UDP; TCP is used for large answers and zone transfers.

visual.caption: The lookup happens before the real connection starts

cards.title: A tree of names
cards.body: Read a name right to left: the root, a top-level domain such as com, then example, then www. Root servers point to TLD servers, which point to each domain's authoritative servers, which hold the records.

visual.caption: www.lab.test read right to left: root, test, lab, www

cards.title: Resolving a name
cards.body: The host hands the whole job to its resolver (a recursive query). The resolver walks down the tree with iterative queries: each server answers or points it one level lower.

frames.caption: Host asks its resolver: www.example.com?
Resolver asks a root server, which says: try the .com servers
Resolver asks a .com server: try example.com's servers
example.com's authoritative server answers: 192.0.2.80
Resolver returns 192.0.2.80 to the host

cards.title: Caching and TTL
cards.body: Resolvers and hosts cache answers. Each record carries a TTL in seconds; until it runs out, repeat lookups come from the cache, not the tree. That is why a changed record can take a while to show up everywhere.

frames.caption: First lookup: the answer is cached with its TTL of 300 seconds
100 seconds later: answered from the cache, no queries sent
After 300 seconds the entry expires; the next lookup walks the tree

cards.title: Record types
cards.body: A zone's records come in types. PTR works backwards: it is the reverse lookup.

visual.caption: NS names an authoritative server for a zone

cards.title: Why NAT
cards.body: Private addresses (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) are not routed on the Internet. NAT, on the edge router or firewall, rewrites them to public ones going out and back coming in. Many hosts share a few public addresses, which helped IPv4 last.

visual.caption: Left of NAT: private 10.1.1.x. Right of it: public 192.0.2.9

cards.title: Cisco's address names
cards.body: Inside or outside says whose address it is; local or global says where it is seen. Outside local is how the outside host looks from inside, usually unchanged.

visual.caption: Inside local is the host's real private address; inside global stands for it outside

cards.title: Three kinds
cards.body: With static NAT the mapping never changes, so outside hosts can start connections to that host. Dynamic NAT lends each host one public address from a pool. PAT (overload) shares one address among many hosts.

visual.caption: Only PAT needs port numbers to tell hosts apart

cards.title: A PAT table
cards.body: Going out, the router swaps the source address and port for its public address and a free port, and records the pair. Coming back, it looks up the reply's destination port and swaps back.

frames.caption: PC .21 sends from port 50100; the router picks free port 1024
PC .22 uses the same source port; it gets public port 1025
A reply arrives for 192.0.2.9:1025; the router finds that port
Destination rewritten to 10.1.1.22:50100, then sent onto the LAN

cards.title: Costs and limits
cards.body: The table is a hash map keyed by address and port. Outside hosts cannot start a connection to a PAT host unless a static mapping is added.

visual.caption: One public address can carry tens of thousands of flows

cards.title: Why time matters
cards.body: Every router, switch and server keeps its own clock. If clocks disagree, logs from different devices can't be lined up, and time checks such as certificate expiry can fail. NTP keeps all clocks close to one good source.

frames.caption: No NTP: one fault, two times. Which came first?
With NTP the time stamps line up: clearly one event

cards.title: How it works
cards.body: A device can be an NTP client and a server at once, passing time on down the line.

visual.caption: Ask, measure the delay, correct, adjust slowly

cards.title: Stratum levels
cards.body: Stratum counts hops from a reference clock such as GPS. Lower means closer to it. Stratum 16 means not synchronized.

frames.caption: Stratum 1: a server fed directly by the reference clock
Clients of a stratum 1 server are stratum 2
Each hop further away adds 1 again: stratum 3

cards.title: Good practice
cards.body: Point each device at two or more NTP servers. Let a few core devices sync from outside and serve the rest. Turn on NTP authentication so a fake server can't shift your clocks.

visual.caption: Two core devices sync from outside; every other device uses both cores

cards.title: Three ways in
cards.body: Three routes reach a device's command line. The console is a cable into the console port; the other two cross the network.

visual.caption: Only the console works with no IP set up at all

cards.title: Why not Telnet
cards.body: Anyone who captures Telnet traffic can read it, user name and password included. SSH has replaced Telnet for managing devices.

visual.caption: Same job, but only SSH hides what you type

cards.title: SSH on Cisco
cards.body: A Cisco switch names its RSA key from its hostname plus domain name, so both must be set before the key can be made. SSH logins need a user name.

ip domain name lab.test

line vty 0 15

cards.title: Setup in order
cards.body: The key's name is built from the hostname plus the domain name, so both must exist before the key can be made.

steps: Create a user name and secret
visual.caption: Hostname and domain name come before the key

cards.title: Remote needs IP
cards.body: Telnet and SSH ride the IP network, so the device needs an IP address (on a switch, on a VLAN interface) and a default gateway to be reached from other subnets. The console needs neither.

frames.caption: SSH from another subnet: the switch needs an IP and a default gateway
Console: the way in on day one or after a bad change

cards.title: SNMP roles
cards.body: An SNMP manager (monitoring software) watches many devices. Each device runs an SNMP agent that keeps values such as interface counters and CPU load in its MIB.

frames.caption: Get: the manager reads values from each agent
Set: the manager changes a value on one agent
Trap or Inform: an agent warns the manager on its own

cards.title: Ports and versions
cards.body: The manager polls agents on UDP 161. Agents send traps to the manager on UDP 162. In v1 and v2c a community string acts as the password.

visual.caption: Only v3 adds users, authentication and encryption

cards.title: Syslog event messages
cards.body: Devices write event messages: a link went down, a login failed. Syslog sends copies to a central server so you can search every device's logs in one place, with NTP keeping the time stamps in line.

visual.caption: Every device sends copies to one server, usually over UDP 514

cards.title: Severity levels
cards.body: Each message has a severity from 0 to 7. Lower number, more serious.

visual.caption: 0 is the worst news; 7 is just debugging detail

cards.title: Choosing a level
cards.body: Picking a level keeps that level and everything more serious.

frames.caption: Level 2 (Critical) keeps 0, 1 and 2
Level 4 (Warning) keeps 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4
Level 7 (Debug) keeps everything

cards.title: How FTP works
cards.body: FTP copies files after a login and can list folders. Commands use a control connection; the file travels on a separate data connection (from port 20 in classic active mode). Everything, password included, is clear text.

steps: Send RETR with the file name
visual.caption: Commands on one connection, file contents on another

cards.title: How TFTP works
cards.body: TFTP is a tiny file copier on UDP port 69, with no login and no folder listing. You name a file and it comes in 512-byte blocks, each acknowledged before the next. Boot-time loaders like that simplicity.

frames.caption: Block 1 (512 bytes) is sent
ACK 1 comes back; only now may the next block go
Block 2 (512 bytes) is sent
ACK 2 comes back
Block 3 (276 bytes) is sent
ACK 3 comes back. Under 512 bytes meant: last block

cards.title: What TFTP costs
cards.body: A file of n bytes takes about n/512 round trips.

visual.caption: One block in memory at a time, so memory stays constant

cards.title: Side by side
cards.body: Neither protocol encrypts anything.

visual.caption: FTP is the full-featured one; TFTP is the bare minimum

cards.title: Finding and securing
cards.body: A device that boots with no settings learns its TFTP server from DHCP: the lease can carry that address. Cisco IP phones fetch their configuration files this way. Safer file transfer exists too.

visual.caption: SFTP rides an SSH session; FTPS wraps FTP in TLS

cards.title: Why layers
cards.body: Networking is split into layers so each part has one job. A layer uses the layer below and serves the layer above. Matching layers on two hosts talk to each other.

visual.caption: Host A's TCP writes a header that only host B's TCP reads

cards.title: The five TCP/IP layers
cards.body: Application: what apps need (HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, POP3). Transport: delivery between programs. Network: addresses and routing over the whole path. Data link: rules for one link. Physical: cables, radio, signals.

visual.caption: Layer 1 is the cable at the bottom; numbers go up from there

cards.title: OSI numbering
cards.body: The older OSI model has seven layers. Its bottom four match TCP/IP in name and number. TCP/IP folds OSI's top three into one application layer, yet people still say 'Layer 7' for a web protocol and 'Layer 3' for IP.

visual.caption: OSI layers 5, 6 and 7 all land in one TCP/IP layer

cards.title: Who does what
cards.body: On a laptop, three parts share the layers. TCP/IP itself is defined in documents called RFCs.

visual.caption: Each part of a laptop owns some of the layers

cards.title: Wrapping data
cards.body: Each layer puts its own header in front of what the layer above handed down. The data-link layer also adds a trailer at the end. This wrapping is encapsulation.

frames.caption: The app hands page data to TCP
TCP adds its header
IP adds its header in front
Ethernet adds a header and a trailer (FCS)
The physical layer sends it all as bits

cards.title: Unwrapping
cards.body: The receiver peels the layers off in reverse order: link first, then IP, then TCP. That is de-encapsulation.

frames.caption: The frame arrives; Ethernet checks and removes its parts
IP reads its header and removes it
TCP reads its header and removes it
The app gets the page data

cards.title: Names for each unit
cards.body: Each layer's unit has a name. PDU (protocol data unit) is the general word for any of them.

visual.caption: Segment inside a packet, packet inside a frame

cards.title: At every router
cards.body: A router checks the frame, drops its link header and trailer, picks the next hop, then wraps the packet in a fresh frame. MACs change on every hop; the IPs stay the same end to end (NAT is the exception).

frames.caption: Hop 1, PC to router 1
Hop 2: new frame, new MACs, same IPs
Hop 3: MACs changed again, IPs never did

cards.title: The Ethernet frame
cards.body: A header, the data, then a trailer. The largest data size, 1500 bytes, is the MTU.

visual.caption: Fields in the order they are sent

cards.title: MAC addresses
cards.body: A MAC is 48 bits (6 bytes), written as 12 hex digits: 3c:52:a1:07:9e:44, or 3c52.a107.9e44 on Cisco. Also called the hardware, physical or burned-in address.

visual.caption: First 3 bytes: maker OUI from the IEEE. Last 3: numbered by the maker

cards.title: Who receives it
cards.body: The destination MAC decides who takes the frame: one interface, everyone, or a group.

frames.caption: Unicast from A: one interface, here B
Broadcast to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff: every device on the LAN
Multicast: only the group that chose to listen, here B and D

cards.title: Catching errors
cards.body: Ethernet detects errors but never resends. TCP, higher up, notices the missing data and has it sent again.

steps: Sender stores a check in FCS
visual.caption: Detecting is Ethernet's job; recovering is TCP's

cards.title: Finding a MAC: ARP
cards.body: To build a frame, a host needs the next device's MAC. Answers stay in an ARP cache for a while, so ARP runs only now and then. On a PC, arp -a lists the cache.

frames.caption: A broadcasts an ARP request: who has 192.168.3.9?
B owns 192.168.3.9, so only B replies, with its MAC
A caches B's MAC and can now send B a frame

cards.title: 32 bits, four octets
cards.body: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers from 0 to 255 with dots between (dotted decimal). Each number is one octet, 8 bits. Every interface that uses IP needs its own address.

visual.caption: 192.0.2.44: each decimal number stands for 8 bits

cards.title: Network and host parts
cards.body: Addresses on one LAN share a prefix (network part); the host part tells them apart. The mask marks the split: 1s over the prefix, 0s over the host. The 1s must all sit on the left, so 255.0.255.0 is illegal.

frames.caption: /24: mask 255.255.255.0. 3 network octets, 1 host
/16: mask 255.255.0.0. 2 network octets, 2 host
/8: mask 255.0.0.0. 1 network octet, 3 host

cards.title: Three mask formats
cards.body: A mask can be binary, dotted decimal, or a prefix: a slash and the count of 1 bits. /21 is 8 + 8 + 5 ones, so 255.255.248.0. A mask octet can only be one of nine values.

visual.caption: Count the 1 bits in an octet, read off its decimal value

cards.title: Private ranges
cards.body: RFC 1918 sets three blocks aside for use inside any organization. Internet routers do not carry them, so NAT translates them at the edge.

cards.title: Old address classes
cards.body: Before CIDR, the first octet fixed the mask. 127.x.x.x is loopback: a host talking to itself. Today any prefix length can be used.

visual.caption: The first octet alone used to decide the mask

cards.title: Counting addresses
cards.body: With H host bits a block holds 2**H addresses. The lowest names the network and the highest is its broadcast, so 2**H - 2 are usable. Python does it in O(1):
cards.code:
import ipaddress
n = ipaddress.ip_network(
    '10.0.0.0/8')
print(n.netmask)  # 255.0.0.0
print(n.num_addresses - 2)
# 16777214

visual.caption: Usable hosts = 2**H - 2

cards.title: What a subnet is
cards.body: A subnet is a run of consecutive addresses that share a prefix. With a /p mask the host part has 32 - p bits. Host bits all 0 give the subnet ID; all 1 give the subnet broadcast. Everything between can go to hosts.

visual.caption: 198.51.100.128/26: ID first, broadcast last, 62 hosts between

cards.title: The block size trick
cards.body: Find the octet where the mask is neither 255 nor 0. Block size = 256 minus that mask octet. Subnet IDs are multiples of it: the multiple at or below the address is the ID; the next multiple minus 1 is the broadcast.

visual.caption: Block size = 256 - mask octet

cards.title: Worked example
cards.body: Find the subnet of 198.51.100.150/26.

frames.caption: Mask /26: the odd octet is 192, so block = 256 - 192 = 64
IDs are multiples of 64. 150 sits between 128 and 192
Subnet 198.51.100.128, broadcast .191, hosts .129 to .190

cards.title: In another octet
cards.body: The trick works in any octet. If the mask is only 255s and 0s, use the octet just after the last 255 (block 256, so that octet becomes 0 and the broadcast ends in 255s).

frames.caption: 172.16.77.9/20: odd octet is the third, block = 256 - 240 = 16
Third-octet multiples of 16: 77 sits between 64 and 80
Subnet ID 172.16.64.0: later octets are 0

cards.title: Check with Python
cards.body: The subnet ID is the address AND the mask, one bit operation: O(1) time and space. Listing every host is O(2**H).
cards.code:
import ipaddress
i = ipaddress.ip_interface(
    '198.51.100.150/26')
n = i.network
print(n)  # 198.51.100.128/26
print(n.broadcast_address)
print(n[1], n[-2])  # usable
print(len(list(n.hosts())))  # 62

cards.title: Same subnet or not
cards.body: Two addresses share a subnet only if they give the same subnet ID under the mask. Looking alike is not enough. Same subnet: talk directly. Different subnets: a router is needed between them.

visual.caption: .30 and .33 are neighbours but sit in different /27 blocks

cards.title: Local or remote
cards.body: Before sending, a host checks whether the destination is in its own subnet. If so, the frame goes straight there. If not, it goes to the default gateway, a router on its own subnet, which carries the packet on.

frames.caption: Same subnet: PC A sends the frame straight to PC B
Other subnet: PC A sends the frame to its default gateway
Routers pass the packet on, hop by hop, to the server

cards.title: The routing table
cards.body: Each router keeps a table of subnets, each with an outgoing interface and often a next-hop router. Routes come from three places.

visual.caption: With a routing protocol, routers tell each other what they reach

cards.title: Most specific wins
cards.body: If several routes match, the router uses the longest prefix. The default route, 0.0.0.0/0, matches everything, so it is used only when nothing else matches. Without one, an unmatched packet is dropped.

frames.caption: 172.16.9.4: 3 routes match; /22 is longest, so R2
172.16.200.1: 2 routes match; /16 is longest, so R1
198.51.100.7: only the default route matches, so R3

cards.title: Lookup in Python
cards.body: This scan checks all n routes: O(n) time and up to O(n) space per packet. Real routers use tries or special hardware to match faster.
cards.code:
import ipaddress as ip
t = {'172.16.0.0/16': 'R1',
     '172.16.8.0/22': 'R2',
     '0.0.0.0/0': 'R3'}
def route(dst):
    d = ip.ip_address(dst)
    hits = [ip.ip_network(r)
        for r in t
        if d in ip.ip_network(r)]
    best = max(hits,
        key=lambda n: n.prefixlen)
    return t[str(best)]
print(route('172.16.9.4'))  # R2

cards.title: Work at each hop
cards.body: A router does the same job on every arriving frame. Only the packet survives from one link to the next.

steps: Wrap packet in a new frame
visual.caption: Check, unwrap, look up, rewrap, send

cards.title: ARP for the gateway
cards.body: For a remote destination the frame still needs a destination MAC, but it is the gateway's, not the far host's. So the host runs ARP for its gateway's IP address.

frames.caption: Host ARPs for the gateway's IP (say 192.168.1.1), not the server's
Frame goes to the gateway's MAC; the packet still names the server's IP
The last router ARPs on the far LAN to learn the server's MAC

cards.title: Two transports
cards.body: TCP fits when every byte matters. UDP fits when late data is useless, or for tiny query-and-answer exchanges.

visual.caption: Reliability on the left, speed and simplicity on the right

cards.title: The three-way handshake
cards.body: TCP opens a connection with three messages. Each side picks a starting sequence number and the other side acknowledges it. Closing uses FIN messages.

frames.caption: SYN: the client sends its starting sequence number
SYN, ACK: the server acks it and sends its own number
ACK: the client acknowledges the server's number
Both sides agree: data can flow

cards.title: Ports pick the program
cards.body: IP gets data to the right host; a 16-bit port (0 to 65535) gets it to the right program. Servers listen on well-known ports; a client picks a fresh temporary port per connection. Four values tell connections apart.

visual.caption: Two connections to one server: only the source port differs

cards.title: Port ranges
cards.body: The 65536 port numbers are split into three ranges.

visual.caption: Servers sit low, client source ports sit high

cards.title: Common ports
cards.body: Worth knowing by heart.

visual.caption: DNS is the UDP one in this list

cards.title: Why IPv6
cards.body: The public IPv4 supply ran out: IANA gave away its last blocks in 2011. NAT and CIDR stretched IPv4, but IPv6 is the long-term fix.

visual.caption: Four times the bits, vastly more addresses

cards.title: Writing an address
cards.body: An IPv6 address is 32 hex digits in eight groups of four, split by colons. 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for examples. Python can shorten or expand one:
cards.code:
import ipaddress
a = ipaddress.ip_address(
    '2001:0db8:0070:0000:'
    '0000:0000:0c00:0001')
print(a)  # 2001:db8:70::c00:1
print(a.exploded)  # full form

visual.caption: Eight groups of four hex digits: 8 x 16 = 128 bits

cards.title: Shortening, step by step
cards.body: Drop leading zeros in each group, then replace one run of two or more all-zero groups with a double colon.

frames.caption: The full address: 32 hex digits
Drop leading zeros: 0db8 is db8, 0000 is 0, 0c00 is c00
The run of three 0 groups becomes ::, giving 2001:db8:70::c00:1

cards.title: Shortening traps
cards.body: To expand again, pad each group to 4 digits and let :: fill in zero groups until there are eight.

left.title: Do
points: Use :: for the longest zero run
If two runs tie, shorten the first

right.title: Don't
points: Drop trailing zeros: 0c00 is not c
Use :: for a single zero group

visual.caption: Two :: would hide how many zero groups each one stands for

cards.title: Prefix length
cards.body: IPv6 writes masks only as a prefix length, /0 to /128. LAN subnets are usually /64: the first 64 bits (4 groups) name the subnet, the last 64 the host. For the prefix, keep the first P bits and set the rest to 0.

frames.caption: Host 2001:db8:70:12:a:b:c:d/64: /64 keeps the first four groups
Set the 64 host bits to 0
Shortened: the subnet prefix is 2001:db8:70:12::/64

cards.title: Same ideas, new parts
cards.body: Hosts still need an address and a default router, and routers still pick the longest matching prefix. Dual stack means a device runs IPv4 and IPv6 side by side.

visual.caption: ICMPv6 replaces ICMP; Neighbor Discovery (NDP) replaces ARP

cards.title: What current is
cards.body: Current is charge flowing past a point. Charge is counted in coulombs (C) and current in amperes (A). One amp means one coulomb passing every second, so I = Q / t and Q = I × t.

visual.caption: Multiply amps by seconds to get coulombs

cards.title: Small units
cards.body: Electronics mostly deals in small currents. A small indicator LED runs on about 20 mA.

visual.caption: Each step down is a thousand times smaller

cards.title: Which way it flows
cards.body: In a metal wire the moving charges are electrons, drifting from the battery's − terminal to +. Diagrams and formulas use conventional current, drawn from + round to −. The maths comes out the same.

frames.caption: Conventional current: drawn from + through the lamp to −
Electrons really drift the opposite way: from − to +

cards.title: Counting electrons
cards.body: One electron carries about 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so one coulomb is roughly 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons. Divide the charge by the electron's charge to count them.
cards.code:
e = 1.602e-19      # C each
amps, secs = 0.5, 4
q = amps * secs    # 2.0 C
print(q / e)       # ~1.25e19

visual.caption: Charge ÷ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives the count

cards.title: Slow drift, fast push
cards.body: A lamp lights the moment the switch closes, even though each electron barely moves.

left.title: Each electron
points: Often well under 1 mm per second

right.title: The push
points: A large fraction of light speed

visual.caption: The signal is fast; the carriers are slow

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: A push between points
cards.body: Voltage is the electrical push that drives current, in volts (V). It always compares two points. One volt means each coulomb moved between them gains or gives up one joule (1 V = 1 J/C), so energy = V × Q.

visual.caption: Volts times coulombs gives joules

cards.title: Ground means 0 V
cards.body: Pick one point, call it ground, and treat it as 0 V. "6 V at node A" means 6 V measured from ground. Between two nodes, subtract their labels. In battery circuits ground is usually the negative terminal.

visual.caption: A meter from A to B reads 6 − 4 = 2 V

cards.title: Stacking batteries
cards.body: Cells joined + to − in series add their voltages. Moving ground to the middle gives a split supply. Cells in parallel keep the same voltage but last longer; only parallel matching, fresh cells.

frames.caption: Ground at the bottom: 4.5 + 4.5 = 9 V at the top
Ground in the middle: a split supply of +4.5 V and −4.5 V

cards.title: One wire, one voltage
cards.body: Every point along a plain wire sits at almost the same voltage, so a voltmeter across a wire reads about 0 V. The voltage is used up across parts that resist current, such as a lamp or a resistor.

visual.caption: Both ends of each wire match; all 9 V drops across the lamp

cards.title: Earth ground
cards.body: The ground symbol can also mean a real link to the earth. A mains outlet's earth pin connects to a rod in the soil, and metal equipment cases are tied to it.

steps: Fault makes a metal case live
Case is tied to the earth pin
Earth pin runs to a soil rod
visual.caption: Why metal cases are earthed

cards.title: Ohm's law
cards.body: Resistance (R) is how strongly a part opposes current, in ohms (Ω). For a resistor, V = I × R, so I = V / R and R = V / I. Some parts, such as diodes, don't follow this straight-line rule.

visual.caption: Straight lines: at 10 V, 100 Ω passes 100 mA but 200 Ω only 50 mA

cards.title: Worked example
bullets: Convert mA to A before dividing: 25 mA = 0.025 A
Volts ÷ kΩ gives mA: 10 V / 2 kΩ = 5 mA

visual.caption: One circuit, three ways to read the same law

cards.title: Shape and material
cards.body: A wire's resistance is R = ρ × L / A. ρ (resistivity, in Ω·m) belongs to the material: copper is about 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, while glass is above 10¹⁰ Ω·m.

visual.caption: Length pushes R up; cross-section area pulls it down

cards.title: Conductors and insulators
cards.body: Heat raises a metal's resistance but lowers a semiconductor's.

visual.caption: Copper is a metal, silicon a semiconductor, glass and rubber insulators

cards.title: Opens and shorts
cards.body: In a short, the current is V divided by the small resistances left in the loop, added together: the wire plus the battery's own internal resistance. It can be huge, which is why fuses exist.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: What power is
cards.body: Power is how fast energy is used, in watts (1 W = 1 joule per second). For any part, multiply the voltage across it by the current through it: P = V × I.

visual.caption: The last row is a 230 V kettle: 2,300 W

cards.title: Power in resistors
cards.body: Put Ohm's law into P = V × I and you get two handy forms: P = I² × R when you know the current, and P = V² / R when you know the voltage. In a resistor all of that power turns into heat.

visual.caption: P = I² × R: 50 mA gives 0.25 W, 100 mA gives 1 W, four times as much

cards.title: Three ways, one answer
cards.body: A 150 Ω resistor carrying 30 mA has 4.5 V across it. Every form of the power law agrees.
cards.code:
i, r = 0.03, 150.0  # 30 mA
v = i * r           # 4.5 V
print(round(v * i, 3))     # VI
print(round(i**2 * r, 3))  # I²R
print(round(v**2 / r, 3))  # V²/R
# all three print 0.135 (W)

visual.caption: Pick the form that matches what you know

cards.title: Power ratings
bullets: Common resistor ratings: 1/8, 1/4, 1/2 and 1 W
Past its rating a resistor overheats and fails
Energy = power × time (joules = watts × seconds)

visual.caption: Rule of thumb: pick at least twice the expected power

cards.title: In series
cards.body: Parts in series sit one after another on a single path. The same current flows through each, their voltages add up to the supply, and the total resistance is the sum: R = R1 + R2 + …

visual.caption: One path, 3 kΩ in all: 4 mA everywhere. Drops: 4 V + 8 V = 12 V

cards.title: In parallel
cards.body: Parts in parallel all connect across the same two points, so each gets the same voltage. The supply current splits between the branches, and the total resistance falls below the smallest branch: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …

visual.caption: Both branches get 12 V. 2 mA + 4 mA = 6 mA, so the pair acts like 2 kΩ

cards.title: Quick rules
bullets: ∥ is short for "in parallel with"
Two in parallel: R1 × R2 / (R1 + R2)
n equal resistors in parallel: R / n

left.title: Series
points: Voltages add up to the supply

cards.body: Shrink a network one piece at a time: replace an obvious series or parallel group with its total, redraw, and repeat. Work from the innermost brackets out.

frames.caption: Start inside the brackets: two equal 200 Ω in parallel
200 ∥ 200 = 200 / 2 = 100 Ω, so the group becomes 100 Ω
What is left is plain series: 100 + 100 = 200 Ω

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Two resistors in series across a supply split its voltage in proportion to their sizes. Take the output from the middle: Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2). R2 sits between the output and ground; R1 goes up to the supply.

visual.caption: R2 is 1 of the 3 kΩ total, so Vout is a third of 12 V: 4 V

cards.title: Worked example
cards.body: Keep Vin at 12 V and change the resistors: the bigger R2's share of the total, the higher Vout.
cards.code:
Vin = 12 V
R1 = 2 kΩ (top)
R2 = 1 kΩ (to ground)
Vout = 12 × 1 / (2 + 1)
     = 4 V

visual.caption: Equal resistors give exactly half the supply

cards.title: Picking R1

cards.title: Loads pull it down
cards.body: A load across the output sits in parallel with R2. That lowers the bottom resistance, so Vout drops. Allow for the load's current when choosing R1, or use a voltage regulator for loads that change.

frames.caption: No load: Vout = 12 × 1 / (2 + 1) = 4 V

cards.title: Current law
cards.body: At any junction, the current flowing in equals the current flowing out. Charge can't pile up or vanish, so the branches must balance.

frames.caption: 40 mA flows in; two of the three ways out carry 15 and 10 mA
In = out: the third wire carries 40 − 15 − 10 = 15 mA

cards.title: Voltage law
cards.body: Go around any closed loop and the voltage rises and drops add to zero. In a single loop, the drops across the parts add up to the source voltage. It is energy bookkeeping: a charge back at its start has gained nothing.

visual.caption: Battery lifts 9 V; R1 drops 3.5 V, R2 the other 5.5 V: sum is 0

cards.title: Current divider
cards.body: When a current splits between two parallel resistors, more goes through the smaller one: I1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2). By the current law, the other branch carries the rest, I − I1.

visual.caption: I1 = 60 × 200 / 300 = 40 mA through the smaller R1; R2 gets the rest

cards.title: Using them
cards.body: For a tricky network, write a current-law equation at each junction and a voltage-law equation around each loop, then solve them together. The laws hold for any parts, including diodes and transistors.

visual.caption: Kirchhoff's two laws work alongside the two you already know

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: DC and AC
cards.body: Direct current (DC) flows one way from a steady source like a battery. Alternating current (AC) keeps reversing, usually as a smooth sine wave. Mains is AC, partly because transformers can change AC voltage efficiently.

visual.caption: DC stays on one side of zero; AC swings above and below it

cards.title: Frequency and period
cards.body: Frequency f is the number of full cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). The period T is the time one cycle takes: T = 1 / f and f = 1 / T.
bullets: A 1 µs period means 1 MHz
US mains: 120 V at 60 Hz; much of the world: 220–240 V at 50 Hz

visual.caption: Two full cycles in 2 ms: T = 1 ms, so f = 1 kHz

cards.title: Peak and peak-to-peak
cards.body: The peak (Vp) is the highest point of the wave, measured from 0 V. Peak-to-peak (Vpp) runs from the lowest point to the highest, so for a sine Vpp = 2 × Vp.

visual.caption: From −10 V up to +10 V: Vpp = 20 V

cards.title: RMS values
cards.body: A sine averages to zero, so it is rated by RMS (square, average, square root): the DC voltage that would heat a resistor just as much. Vrms = Vp / √2 ≈ 0.707 × Vp, and Vp ≈ 1.414 × Vrms. Mains ratings like 120 V are RMS.

frames.caption: Equal time above and below zero: a plain average gives 0
Square it: never negative now, and the average is 50
Square root of 50 is 7.07 V: the RMS, at 0.707 of the peak

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
import math
vrms = 230
vp = vrms * math.sqrt(2)
print(round(vp, 1))      # 325.3
print(round(2 * vp, 1))  # 650.5

visual.caption: The code below works out the 230 V row

cards.title: AC power in resistors
cards.body: With RMS values, Ohm's law and the power formulas work on a plain resistor just as for DC: Irms = Vrms / R, and P = Vrms² / R gives the average power.

visual.caption: Using the peak voltage doubles the answer

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: Wire gauge
cards.body: Wire thickness is given as a gauge number (AWG in the US). The scale runs backwards: a smaller number means a thicker wire. Thicker wire has less resistance and carries more current; an overloaded thin wire heats up and can melt.

visual.caption: Diameter in mm for each AWG number: bigger number, thinner wire

cards.title: Solid or stranded
cards.body: Magnet wire is a third kind: varnish-coated, for winding coils.

cards.title: Poles and throws
cards.body: A pole is one separate circuit the switch controls; a throw is each contact a pole can connect to. S means single (1) and D means double (2).

visual.caption: A DPDT works two circuits at once, each choosing between two contacts

cards.title: Throwing a switch
cards.body: An SPDT switch has one pole (the common contact) and two throws. Flipping it moves the connection from one throw to the other.

frames.caption: Lever up: common connects to throw A; B is disconnected
Lever down: common connects to throw B instead

cards.title: Push buttons
cards.body: Momentary switches spring back when you let go. Some toggle switches also have a center-off position.

visual.caption: NO connects only while pressed; NC breaks only while pressed

cards.title: Special switches
bullets: Reed switch: two thin contacts in glass that close near a magnet (door alarms)
DIP switch: a row of tiny switches that fits a chip socket
Rotary switch: one pole, many throws, e.g. SP8T

visual.caption: Three switches for special jobs

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: What a relay is
cards.body: A relay is a switch worked by electricity. A small, low-voltage control circuit can switch a separate, bigger circuit, and the two stay electrically apart.

frames.caption: A low-voltage control circuit drives the coil
Current in a coil makes a magnetic field
The contact is spring-loaded and moves over
The big circuit never touches the control circuit

steps: Coil off: spring pulls it back
frames.caption: With no magnet, the contact returns

cards.title: Kinds of relay
bullets: Contacts are named like switches: SPDT, NO, NC
Coils are rated for a voltage, such as 5, 12 or 24 V DC

visual.caption: Fewer moving parts, faster switching

cards.title: The flyback diode
cards.body: A relay coil is an inductor and fights any sudden change in current. Switch it off and it can kick out a spike of hundreds of volts, enough to destroy the transistor driving it. A diode across the coil gives it a safe loop.

frames.caption: Transistor switch on: current runs through the coil; the diode blocks
Switch off: the coil's current loops through the diode and dies away

cards.title: Fuses and breakers
cards.body: Both protect wiring and parts from shorts and overloads by opening the circuit when the current goes past a rating.

cards.title: Choosing a fuse
bullets: Fast-blow: opens on a brief surge; for sensitive electronics
Slow-blow (time-lag): rides out turn-on surges from motors
On mains, put it in the hot (live) wire, before the device, so a blown fuse cuts off the live voltage

visual.caption: Multiply the normal current by 1.5

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: Color digits
cards.body: Small through-hole resistors are marked with colored bands. Each color stands for a digit.

visual.caption: Ten colors for the digits 0 to 9

cards.title: Reading four bands
cards.body: Start from the end away from the gold or silver band. Bands 1 and 2 are digits, band 3 is the multiplier (how many zeros to add, a power of ten), and band 4 is the tolerance.

frames.caption: Hold it with the gold band on the right, then read from the left
Band 1 is a digit: green = 5
Band 2 is a digit: blue = 6, so 56 so far
Band 3 is the multiplier: red = 2 zeros, × 100
Band 4 is the tolerance: gold = ±5%

cards.title: Tolerance bands
cards.body: Gold or silver can also appear as band 3: there they multiply by 0.1 or 0.01.

visual.caption: Brown and red mark precision parts

cards.title: Five bands
cards.body: Precision resistors often carry five bands: three digits, then the multiplier, then the tolerance.

frames.caption: Five bands: the first three are digits: 1, 5, 0
Band 4 is the multiplier: red = × 100
Band 5 is the tolerance: brown = ±1%

cards.title: What tolerance means
cards.body: Tolerance is how far the real value may be from the printed one. 5% of 470 Ω is 23.5 Ω either way. For most hobby circuits ±5% is fine.

visual.caption: Take the percentage of the printed value, then go below and above

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: C.index(color) is the color's digit. The lookup scans a fixed list of ten colors: O(1) time and space.
cards.code:
C = ["black", "brown", "red",
     "orange", "yellow", "green",
     "blue", "violet", "gray",
     "white"]

def ohms(b1, b2, b3):
    i = C.index
    n = 10 * i(b1) + i(b2)
    return n * 10 ** i(b3)

print(ohms("green", "blue", "red"))
# 5600

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: Storing charge
cards.body: A capacitor is two conducting plates with an insulator between them. Put a voltage across it and it stores charge: Q = C × V. Capacitance C is in farads (F); real parts run from a few pF to tens of thousands of µF.

visual.caption: More capacitance or more voltage means more stored charge

cards.title: DC blocked, AC passed
cards.body: Once charged, a capacitor lets no steady DC through. Changing signals pass more easily at higher frequency: reactance Xc = 1 / (2πfC) ohms. In series it blocks DC between stages; from supply to ground it drains noise.

visual.caption: About 3.2 kΩ at 50 Hz, only 159 Ω at 1 kHz: higher f, less opposition

cards.title: Combining capacitors
cards.body: The rules are the opposite of the resistor rules. A parallel group is limited by its lowest voltage rating.

visual.caption: Parallel adds; series (1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2) is smaller than either

cards.title: RC time constant
cards.body: Charging through a resistor takes time. The time constant is τ = R × C (ohms × farads = seconds): 10 kΩ × 100 µF = 1 s. Charging from 0 V: V = Vs × (1 − e^(−t/τ)). Discharging: V = V0 × e^(−t/τ).

visual.caption: At one τ, charging reaches 63.2% and discharging has fallen to 36.8%

cards.title: Tau by tau
cards.body: Each time constant closes 63.2% of the remaining gap, so the voltage is about full after five.
cards.code:
import math
for n in range(1, 6):
    pct = 100 * (1 - math.exp(-n))
    print(n, round(pct, 1))
# 63.2 86.5 95.0 98.2 99.3

frames.caption: After 1 time constant: 63.2% of the supply
After 2 time constants: 86.5% of the supply
After 3 time constants: 95.0% of the supply
After 4 time constants: 98.2% of the supply
After 5 time constants: 99.3% of the supply (about full)

cards.title: Electrolytics have polarity
cards.body: Reverse an electrolytic, or go past its voltage rating, and it can overheat, leak or burst.

left.title: Electrolytic
points: Large values in a small can

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: What an inductor is
cards.body: An inductor is a coil of wire, often on an iron or ferrite core. It resists any change in its current: the faster the change, the bigger the voltage it develops (V = L × ΔI / Δt). Inductance L is in henrys (H).

visual.caption: Same 1 A change, done faster: a far bigger voltage

cards.title: AC versus DC
cards.body: Steady DC passes, meeting only the wire's small resistance. AC is opposed more as frequency rises: XL = 2πfL ohms. That is the opposite of a capacitor, and why coils work as chokes against high-frequency noise.

visual.caption: The coil's reactance climbs in step with frequency; the capacitor's falls

cards.title: Combining coils
cards.body: Inductors combine like resistors, as long as the coils don't share magnetic field. Cutting a coil's current suddenly causes a voltage spike.

visual.caption: Series adds; parallel (1/L = 1/L1 + 1/L2) is smaller than either

cards.title: How transformers work
cards.body: A transformer is two coils on one iron core. Steady DC makes no changing field, so a transformer can't convert it.

steps: AC flows in the primary coil
visual.caption: The turns ratio sets the voltage ratio

cards.title: Turns ratio
cards.body: Vs = Vp × Ns / Np. Fewer turns on the secondary steps the voltage down; more turns steps it up.

visual.caption: Row 3 has more secondary turns, so it steps up

cards.title: Current trades off
cards.body: An ideal transformer passes on all its power, so Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. Step the voltage down and the current steps up by the same ratio: Is / Ip = Np / Ns. Real ones waste some power as heat.

visual.caption: Voltage down 20 times, current up 20 times, same power

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: A one-way valve
cards.body: A diode lets current through in one direction only. It has an anode (the p side) and a cathode (the n side, marked with a band).

cards.title: Forward voltage
bullets: Silicon: about 0.6–0.7 V before it conducts
Schottky: about 0.4 V, and faster
Germanium: about 0.2–0.3 V
Diodes in series add their drops
Limits: max forward current and peak reverse voltage (PIV)

visual.caption: Almost no current until about 0.6 V, then it shoots up

cards.title: AC to DC
cards.body: A rectifier turns AC into DC. One diode (half-wave) passes only the positive halves. A bridge of four diodes uses both halves, but the current always crosses two diodes. A capacitor after it smooths the ripple.

frames.caption: One cycle of AC in (6 V RMS): half above zero, half below
One diode: only the positive half gets through, one drop lower
Bridge: both halves come out positive, two drops below the peak

cards.title: Bridge example
cards.body: The output peak of a bridge is two diode drops below the input peak.

visual.caption: Start from the peak, not the RMS value

cards.title: Other diode jobs
bullets: Series diode: blocks a battery put in backwards
Flyback diode: soaks up a coil's switch-off spike
Zener diode: conducts in reverse at a set voltage, for simple regulators

visual.caption: Three more uses for the one-way valve

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 4

cards.title: Light from a diode
cards.body: An LED is a diode built to give off light when forward-biased. Like any diode it conducts one way only. Brightness follows the current.

cards.title: Forward voltage
cards.body: Typical current is 10–30 mA; assume 20 mA if unsure.

visual.caption: White and blue need the most voltage

cards.title: The series resistor
cards.body: An LED hardly limits its own current: a little above its forward voltage the current shoots up and burns it out. So add a resistor in series: R = (Vsupply − Vled) / I, then round up to the next standard value.
cards.code:
12 V supply, LED drops 3.4 V
want 20 mA
R = (12 - 3.4) / 0.02
  = 430 Ω

visual.caption: The resistor takes the spare 12 − 3.4 = 8.6 V at 20 mA

cards.title: Several LEDs
cards.body: LEDs in series can share one resistor: subtract all their forward voltages from the supply first. Don't run LEDs in parallel from a single resistor; whichever warms up takes more of the current.

frames.caption: Series: R = (12 − 2 − 2) / 0.02 = 400 Ω, one resistor for both
Parallel: give each LED its own resistor, (5 − 2) / 0.02 = 150 Ω

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 5

cards.title: Small controls big
cards.body: A transistor uses a small signal on one lead to control a larger current through the other two, like a hand on a tap. The two big families are bipolar transistors (BJTs) and field-effect transistors (FETs).

left.title: As a switch
points: Turns a load on and off

cards.title: NPN basics
cards.body: An NPN bipolar transistor has a base (B), a collector (C) and an emitter (E). It turns on when current flows into the base, which sits about 0.6–0.7 V above the emitter. A PNP works the same with every polarity flipped.

visual.caption: A small current into the base lets a big one flow from C to E

cards.title: Current gain
cards.body: In its active region a small base current controls a bigger collector current: Ic = β × Ib. The gain β (also written hFE) varies by part, typically 10 to 500. Both currents leave through the emitter: Ie = Ib + Ic.

visual.caption: The collector current is β times the base current

cards.title: Three regions
cards.body: Cutoff and saturation make a switch; the active region makes an amplifier.

visual.caption: In the active region small changes come out bigger

cards.title: As a switch
cards.body: To switch a load, find the base current it needs, Ib = Ic / β, and size the base resistor from the control voltage: Rb = (Vin − 0.7) / Ib. Pick a somewhat smaller resistor so it is surely saturated.

frames.caption: Vin 0 V: no base current, so cutoff. No collector current: load off
Vin 5 V: about 2.4 mA into the base saturates it; 200 mA flows

cards.title: Field-effect transistors (MOSFETs)
cards.body: A common n-channel enhancement MOSFET is off with 0 V on its gate and turns on once the gate is a few volts above the source. FETs are the workhorse of modern chips.

right.title: MOSFET
points: On: gate a few V above source

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 4

cards.title: Two kinds of signal
cards.body: An analog signal can take any value in a range, like a thermometer voltage drifting from 0.31 V to 0.47 V. A digital signal uses just two levels, HIGH and LOW, so each wire carries one bit.

visual.caption: The smooth line takes any value; the square one only two

cards.title: Why go digital
cards.body: Two clean levels are easy to tell apart, so digital circuits can store bits and make logical decisions, which plain analog circuits can't.

cards.title: Logic levels
bullets: Negative true logic swaps them: LOW means true
Each logic family sets its own valid voltage bands; a voltage between them is not a valid level

visual.caption: Positive true logic: HIGH = 1 = true

cards.title: The clock
cards.body: A clock signal flips between HIGH and LOW over and over, f times per second. One full cycle takes T = 1/f seconds, and circuits do their work when it switches.

visual.caption: One full cycle (HIGH then LOW) takes 20 ns

cards.title: Serial or parallel
cards.body: Serial sends a word down one wire, one bit per clock period: n bits take n periods, O(n) time. Parallel gives every bit its own wire and moves the word in one period, but needs n wires.
cards.code:
12-bit word, T = 100 ns
serial:   12 x 100 = 1200 ns
parallel:  1 x 100 =  100 ns

frames.caption: Period 1: bit 1 is on the wire
Period 2: bit 0 is on the wire
Period 3: bit 1 is on the wire
Period 4: bit 1 is on the wire
Serial took 4 periods. Parallel: 4 wires, 1 period

cards.title: Logic families
bullets: Fanout: how many same-family inputs one output can drive
Propagation delay: time from an input change to the output change, in nanoseconds

visual.caption: Two families of logic chips

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Place values
cards.body: Binary uses only 0 and 1. Each place is worth twice the place on its right. The leftmost bit is the most significant (MSB), the rightmost the least (LSB). Add the values under every 1.

cards.title: Decimal to binary
cards.body: Divide by 2 again and again and keep each remainder. The first remainder is the LSB and the last one is the MSB, so the bits fill in from the right.

frames.caption: 37 / 2 = 18 remainder 1 (LSB)
18 / 2 = 9 remainder 0
9 / 2 = 4 remainder 1
4 / 2 = 2 remainder 0
2 / 2 = 1 remainder 0
1 / 2 = 0 remainder 1 (MSB)
Quotient is 0, so stop: 37 = 100101

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: divmod(n, 2) gives the whole quotient n // 2 and the remainder n % 2. One loop pass per bit: O(log n) time, and O(log n) space for the digits.

cards.title: Hexadecimal (base 16)
cards.body: Hex is base 16: digits 0 to 9, then A to F for 10 to 15. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits.

cards.title: Binary to hex
cards.body: Split the bits into groups of 4 from the right (pad with 0s on the left) and swap each group for its digit. Octal does the same with groups of 3. Going back: 0x3A = 0011 1010 = 58.

frames.caption: Split into groups of 4 bits, starting from the right

cards.title: Handy facts
bullets: Decimal to hex: divide by 16 and keep the remainders, like with 2
Python: hex(235) gives '0xeb', int('EB', 16) gives 235

visual.caption: Every 4 bits make one hex digit

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Binary-coded decimal
cards.body: BCD stores each decimal digit in its own 4-bit group. It suits digit displays like clocks and meters. Only 0000 to 1001 (0 to 9) are valid groups; 1010 to 1111 never appear.

visual.caption: Each digit of 407 gets its own 4 bits

cards.title: BCD is not binary
cards.body: Converting digit by digit is not the same as converting the whole number. BCD needs more bits for the same value: 407 is 12 bits in BCD but 9 bits (1 1001 0111) in binary.

visual.caption: Same number, different bit patterns

cards.title: Two's complement
cards.body: Circuits store negatives in two's complement. Positives are plain binary. For a negative, write the positive value, flip every bit (the one's complement), then add 1.

frames.caption: Flip every bit: the one's complement
Add 1: 1111 0111 is -9. The top bit 1 means negative

cards.title: Reading the sign
cards.body: The top bit shows the sign: 1 means negative. 8 bits hold -128 to +127. Sign-magnitude, which only sets the top bit (-9 would be 1000 1001), is rarely used for math.

visual.caption: Every pattern starting with 1 is negative

cards.title: Adding in binary
cards.body: Add columns from the right: 0+1 = 1, 1+1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1), 1+1+1 = 11 (write 1, carry 1). n-bit numbers take n column steps: O(n).

frames.caption: Column 1: 0+1 = 1: write 1, no carry
Column 2: 1+1 = 10: write 0, carry 1
Column 4: 1+0+1 = 10: write 0, carry 1
Column 8: 0+0+1 = 1: write 1, no carry

cards.title: Subtract by adding
cards.body: With two's complement, subtracting is adding the negative; drop any carry out of the top bit. Python's & 0xFF keeps the low 8 bits.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: What a gate does
cards.body: A logic gate takes one or more input bits and gives one output bit. A truth table lists the output for every input combination. n inputs give 2ⁿ rows, so writing out a full table takes O(2ⁿ) time.

visual.caption: Each extra input doubles the rows

cards.title: The basic gates
bullets: NOT: flips its one input
AND: 1 only if every input is 1
OR: 1 if at least one input is 1
XOR: 1 if the two inputs differ

visual.caption: Find the 1s: AND has one, OR three, XOR the two mixed rows

cards.title: Flipped outputs
cards.body: NAND, NOR and XNOR are AND, OR and XOR with the output flipped. Step through and compare each pair of columns.

frames.caption: NOT has one input and flips it
NAND is 0 only when every input is 1
NOR is 1 only when every input is 0
XNOR is 1 when the two inputs are equal

cards.title: More inputs
cards.body: AND, OR, NAND and NOR also come with 3, 4 or 8 inputs. A 4-input AND gives 1 in only one of its 16 rows (all 1s), and a 4-input OR gives 0 in only one row (all 0s). NAND and NOR flip those, so their counts swap.

visual.caption: 16 rows each: flipping the output swaps the counts

cards.title: Gates in Python
cards.body: On the bits 0 and 1, Python's & is AND, | is OR and ^ is XOR. 1 - x flips a bit.
cards.code:
a, b = 1, 0
print(a & b)        # AND  0
print(a | b)        # OR   1
print(a ^ b)        # XOR  1
print(1 - a)        # NOT  0
print(1 - (a & b))  # NAND 1
print(int(a == b))  # XNOR 0

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

visual.caption: + is OR, so 1 + 1 = 1. Books draw A' as a bar over A

cards.title: Handy identities
cards.body: Each OR rule has an AND twin. Two more worth knowing: A + A·B = A (absorption) and A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C.

visual.caption: Row 4: a thing OR its opposite is 1; AND its opposite is 0

cards.title: Simplifying an expression
cards.body: Fewer terms mean fewer gates. Factor out what the terms share, then apply the identities.

frames.caption: Y' appears in both terms
Factor out the shared Y'
X + X' = 1: a thing OR its opposite
1·Y' = Y': the output ignores X

cards.title: De Morgan's laws
cards.body: To split a bar over a group, flip each variable and swap AND with OR. So a NAND acts like an OR with inverted inputs, and a NOR like an AND with inverted inputs. This is called bubble pushing.

frames.caption: NAND = OR of the inverted inputs: the columns match
NOR = AND of the inverted inputs: the columns match

cards.title: Check every row
cards.body: Two expressions are equal if they agree on every row. With n variables that is 2ⁿ rows: O(2ⁿ) time.
cards.code:
rows = [(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)]
for a, b in rows:
    assert 1-(a|b) == (1-a)&(1-b)
print('De Morgan holds')

cards.title: Universal gates
cards.body: NAND alone can build every other gate, and so can NOR. Simplified designs usually end up as a sum of products (ORed AND terms, like A·B + C) or a product of sums; Karnaugh maps help find the simplest.

frames.caption: Tie a NAND's inputs together and it becomes NOT
Put that NOT after a NAND and you get AND

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: No memory
cards.body: In combinational logic the output depends only on the inputs right now. Common blocks come ready-made as chips.

visual.caption: Nothing is stored: same inputs, same output, every time

cards.title: Mux and demux
cards.body: A multiplexer (mux) uses n select lines to choose one of 2ⁿ inputs and pass it to its one output. A demultiplexer does the reverse: it sends one input to one of 2ⁿ outputs.

frames.caption: Select 00 passes D0 to the output Y
Select 01 passes D1 to the output Y
Select 10 passes D2 to the output Y
Select 11 passes D3 to the output Y

cards.title: Decoder and encoder
cards.body: A decoder turns an n-bit code into exactly one active line out of 2ⁿ. An encoder is the reverse: the one active input becomes its binary code. A priority encoder picks the highest if several are active.

visual.caption: 2-to-4 decoder: each code turns on one line (H)

cards.title: Active-low outputs
cards.body: Many decoders mark the chosen line by pulling it LOW while every other line stays HIGH. A bubble on the pin, or a bar over its name, shows this.

visual.caption: Active-low: code 10 makes only Y2 LOW

cards.title: Half and full adders
cards.body: A half adder adds two bits: sum = A XOR B, carry = A AND B. A full adder also takes a carry in: two half adders (A with B, then that sum with the carry in) plus an OR that merges their carries.
cards.code:
def half_add(a, b):
    return a ^ b, a & b

print(half_add(1, 1))  # (0, 1)
print(half_add(1, 0))  # (1, 0)

frames.caption: Half adder: 1 + 1 = 10, so sum 0 and carry 1
Full adder: Cout is 1 when two or more inputs are 1

cards.title: Ripple-carry adder
cards.body: Chain n full adders, each carry out feeding the next carry in. The top stage must wait for the carry to ripple through every stage: worst case n stage delays, O(n) time, using O(n) gates. 8 stages at 5 ns: 40 ns.

frames.caption: Stage 1 done after 5 ns: sum 0, carry out 1
Stage 2 done after 10 ns: sum 0, carry out 1
Stage 3 done after 15 ns: sum 0, carry out 1
Stage 4 done after 20 ns: sum 1, carry out 0

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Logic with memory
cards.body: Sequential logic stores bits, so its output depends on past inputs as well as present ones. The basic one-bit store is a latch or flip-flop. A clock usually decides when it takes in new data.

cards.title: SR latch
cards.body: Two cross-coupled NOR gates with inputs S (set) and R (reset). S = R = 1 forces both outputs to 0, and the state after release is a race, so it is avoided. A NAND latch has active-low inputs: its hold state is 1 1.

visual.caption: With S = R = 0 the latch keeps whatever it stored

cards.title: Level vs edge
cards.body: A level-triggered (gated) latch follows its inputs the whole time its clock or enable is HIGH. An edge-triggered flip-flop looks only at the instant the clock rises (or falls) and ignores changes at any other time.

visual.caption: D rises while the clock is HIGH: the latch follows, the flip-flop waits

cards.title: D flip-flop
cards.body: A D flip-flop feeds D to S and an inverted copy to R, so S = R = 1 can't happen. At each active clock edge Q takes the value of D; between edges Q holds. D must be steady for a short setup time before the edge.

frames.caption: Edge 1: Q copies D = 1, so Q goes 0 to 1
Edge 2: Q copies D = 1 (no change)
Edge 3: Q copies D = 0, so Q goes 1 to 0
Edge 4: Q copies D = 1, so Q goes 0 to 1

cards.title: JK flip-flop
cards.body: JK works like SR, but J = K = 1 toggles instead of being forbidden: Q flips on every active edge.

visual.caption: Only the last row differs from the SR latch

cards.title: Tracing a JK
cards.body: Q starts at 1. Apply one row of the JK table at each clock edge.

frames.caption: Edge 1: J K = 0 1 is reset, so Q goes 1 to 0
Edge 2: J K = 1 1 is toggle, so Q goes 0 to 1
Edge 3: J K = 0 0 is hold, so Q goes 1 to 1
Edge 4: J K = 1 1 is toggle, so Q goes 1 to 0

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Counting with toggles
cards.body: A flip-flop in toggle mode flips once per clock edge, so its output runs at half the clock frequency. Chain n, each clocked by the one before, for a ripple counter: it counts 0 to 2ⁿ - 1 (MOD-2ⁿ) and divides the clock by 2ⁿ.

frames.caption: Count 0
Count 1: Q0 flips on every clock edge
Count 2
Count 3
Count 4
Count 5
Count 6
Count 7: all 1s, the next edge wraps to 0

cards.title: Sizing a counter
cards.body: n flip-flops give 2ⁿ states. Each stage also halves the frequency: 100 kHz into 4 stages comes out at 100 / 16 = 6.25 kHz.

visual.caption: States double with each flip-flop; the top count is states - 1

cards.title: Ripple vs synchronous
cards.body: In a ripple counter delays add up: 4 stages of 25 ns settle 100 ns after the edge, O(n) for n stages. A synchronous counter uses gates to pick which flip-flops toggle.

cards.title: Shift registers
cards.body: A row of D flip-flops where each Q feeds the next D. On each clock edge every bit moves one place, so loading n bits serially takes n clocks.
bullets: Serial-in, serial-out: delays a bit stream
Serial-in, parallel-out: collects bits into a word
Parallel-in, serial-out: sends a word one bit per clock

frames.caption: A 4-bit register, empty. Bits 1, 0, 1 will enter on the left
Clock 1: 1 enters, every bit moves one place right
Clock 2: 0 enters, every bit moves one place right
Clock 3: 1 enters, every bit moves one place right

cards.title: Ring and Johnson
cards.body: Feed the last output back to the first input and a single 1 goes round: a ring counter of n flip-flops has n states (100, 010, 001). Feed back the inverted last output instead for a Johnson counter with 2n states.

frames.caption: Start: all 0s
Clock 1: the inverted last bit (1) enters on the left
Clock 2: the inverted last bit (1) enters on the left
Clock 3: the inverted last bit (1) enters on the left
Clock 4: the inverted last bit (0) enters on the left
Clock 5: the inverted last bit (0) enters on the left
Back to 000 after 6 states (2 x 3)

cards.title: Shifting in Python
cards.body: A list can model a register. Each shift copies the list: O(n) time and space per clock, though hardware moves all bits at once. To shift right instead, use [bit] + reg[:-1].
cards.code:
reg = [0, 0, 0]
for bit in [1, 1, 0]:
    reg = reg[1:] + [bit]  # left
    print(reg)

frames.caption: 1 enters on the right; the others move left: prints [0, 0, 1]
1 enters on the right; the others move left: prints [0, 1, 1]
0 enters on the right; the others move left: prints [1, 1, 0]

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Tables and queries
cards.body: A table stores rows, and every row has the same named columns. A SELECT query describes the rows and columns you want; the database works out how to fetch them. Keywords are not case-sensitive, and a statement ends with a semicolon. The examples use this songs table:
cards.code:
id title artist year plays
1  Glow  1      2019 420
2  Drift 1      2021 150
3  Tide  2      1998 900
4  Spark 2      2022 NULL
5  Echo  NULL   2005 60

cards.title: Pick and filter
cards.code:
SELECT title, plays
FROM songs
WHERE year >= 2000
  AND plays > 100;
-- Glow 420, Drift 150
cards.body: SELECT lists the columns (* means all), FROM names the table, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. AND binds tighter than OR, so use parentheses when you mix them.

cards.title: Handy filters
bullets: IN (1, 3): matches any value in the list.
BETWEEN 2019 AND 2021: a range that includes both ends.
LIKE 'D%': % stands for any run of characters, _ for exactly one. In SQLite, LIKE ignores case for plain letters.
DISTINCT: drops duplicate rows from the result.

cards.title: Sorting and limits
cards.code:
SELECT title, year
FROM songs
ORDER BY year DESC
LIMIT 2;
-- Spark 2022, Drift 2021
cards.body: ORDER BY sorts ascending unless you add DESC; extra columns break ties. LIMIT n keeps the first n rows (SQL Server uses TOP instead). Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed.

cards.title: Clause order, cost
cards.body: Write clauses in this order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT. With no index, WHERE has to scan every row: O(n) time. ORDER BY needs a sort, O(n log n) time and O(n) space, unless an index already keeps that order.

cards.title: Unknown, not zero
cards.body: NULL marks a missing or unknown value. It is not 0 and not the empty string ''. Comparing anything with NULL, even NULL = NULL, gives NULL (unknown), and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. So unknown rows quietly drop out.

cards.title: Test with IS
cards.body: Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL; = NULL never matches.

cards.title: Three-valued logic
bullets: TRUE AND NULL is NULL; FALSE AND NULL is FALSE.
TRUE OR NULL is TRUE; FALSE OR NULL is NULL.
NOT NULL is still NULL.
So WHERE x <> 5 also skips rows where x is NULL.

cards.title: Filling the gaps
cards.body: COALESCE(a, b, ...) returns its first argument that is not NULL. SQLite also has IFNULL(a, b) for two arguments. Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: 5 + NULL is NULL.
cards.code:
SELECT title,
  COALESCE(plays, 0)
FROM songs;
-- Spark shows 0

cards.title: Aggregate functions
cards.code:
SELECT COUNT(*),      -- 5
       COUNT(plays),  -- 4
       SUM(plays),    -- 1530
       AVG(plays)     -- 382.5
FROM songs;
cards.body: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip NULLs, so AVG divides by 4 here, not 5.

cards.title: Grouping rows
cards.body: GROUP BY puts rows with the same value into one group and returns one row per group. Each selected column should be grouped or wrapped in an aggregate; SQLite is looser and lets other columns through, but their values come from just one row of the group.

cards.title: WHERE versus HAVING
cards.code:
SELECT artist_id,
       COUNT(*) AS n
FROM songs
WHERE year > 2000
GROUP BY artist_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
-- artist 1, n = 2
cards.body: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after the aggregates exist, so COUNT(*) belongs in HAVING; in WHERE it is an error.

cards.title: Run order, cost
cards.body: The database runs FROM, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY and LIMIT. Grouping by sorting costs O(n log n) time; grouping with a hash table costs O(n) average time and O(g) space for g groups.

cards.title: Why join
cards.body: Data is split over tables that point at each other with keys: songs.artist_id holds an id from artists. A join puts matching rows side by side, and ON gives the matching rule. Short aliases (FROM songs AS s) keep column names clear: s.title. Artists here: 1 Nova, 2 Lumen, 3 Quill.

cards.title: INNER JOIN
cards.code:
SELECT s.title, a.name
FROM songs AS s
JOIN artists AS a
  ON a.id = s.artist_id;
-- 4 rows; Echo has no
-- artist, so it is left out
cards.body: Plain JOIN means INNER JOIN: only rows with a match on both sides.

cards.title: LEFT JOIN
cards.code:
SELECT a.name, s.title
FROM artists AS a
LEFT JOIN songs AS s
  ON s.artist_id = a.id;
-- 5 rows: Nova 2, Lumen 2,
-- Quill once, title NULL
cards.body: Every row of the left table stays. Where nothing matches, the right side's columns are NULL. Add WHERE s.id IS NULL to keep only the rows with no match: Quill.

cards.title: What joins cost
cards.body: A nested-loop join with no index compares every pair: O(n·m) time for tables of n and m rows. With an index on the inner table's join column it is about O(n log m). A join with no matching rule (CROSS JOIN) returns all n·m pairs.

cards.title: Adding rows
cards.body: List the columns, then VALUES with one value per column. Columns you leave out get their default, or NULL. You can add several rows at once: VALUES (...), (...).

cards.title: Changing rows
cards.body: SET gives the new values and WHERE picks the rows. A row whose plays is NULL stays NULL, since NULL + 10 is NULL.

cards.title: Removing rows
cards.code:
DELETE FROM songs
WHERE year < 2000;
cards.body: DELETE removes rows but keeps the table; DROP TABLE removes the table itself.

cards.title: Mind the WHERE
bullets: UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE hits every row.
Run the WHERE in a SELECT first to see which rows match.
Wrap risky changes in BEGIN ... COMMIT, or ROLLBACK to undo.
Cost: finding rows is O(n) without an index, and each change also updates every index on the table.

cards.title: Primary keys
cards.body: A primary key is a column, or set of columns, whose value picks out exactly one row. The database rejects a duplicate. In SQLite an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column fills itself in with the next number when you leave it out of an INSERT.

cards.title: Foreign keys
cards.body: A foreign key column holds a key from another table, for example songs.artist_id pointing at artists.id. With checks on, the database refuses a child row whose parent doesn't exist, and by default refuses to delete a parent that rows still point at. A NULL foreign key is allowed.

cards.title: Turn checks on
cards.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=1")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE a(id INTEGER
  PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE b(a_id INTEGER
  REFERENCES a(id));""")
try:
    db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO b VALUES (99)")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print(e)  # FOREIGN KEY ...
cards.body: SQLite leaves foreign key checks off unless each connection runs PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON (or = 1), outside a transaction.

cards.title: Other constraints
bullets: NOT NULL: the column must have a value.
UNIQUE: no two rows share the value.
CHECK (plays >= 0): every row must pass the test.
DEFAULT 0: the value used when none is given.

cards.title: A sorted lookup
cards.body: An index is a separate, sorted copy of one or more columns, with a pointer to each row, like the index at the back of a book. SQLite stores it as a B-tree. UNIQUE and primary key columns are indexed for you (an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the table's own sort key).
cards.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_songs_year
ON songs(year);

cards.title: Why it is faster
cards.body: Without an index, finding rows means a full table scan: O(n). With one, the database searches the tree in O(log n) and then fetches the matching rows. Range filters, joins and ORDER BY on that column can use it too. An index on (a, b) helps queries on a, or a and b, but usually not on b alone.

cards.title: See the plan
cards.code:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM songs
WHERE year = 2021;
-- no index: SCAN songs
-- with it:  SEARCH songs
--   USING INDEX idx_songs_year
cards.body: SCAN means every row is read; SEARCH means an index narrows it down.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Extra storage: O(n) space per index.
Slower writes: each INSERT, DELETE, or UPDATE of an indexed column also updates the index, O(log n) per index.
A plain index allows duplicates; only UNIQUE refuses them.
Index columns you often search, join or sort on, not every column.

cards.title: Each fact once
cards.body: Normalizing means splitting tables so each fact is stored in one place. Here Ana's town is copied into every order she makes:
cards.code:
orders
id name town  item
1  Ana  Leeds pen
2  Ana  Leeds ink
3  Ben  York  pad

cards.title: Three anomalies
bullets: Update: Ana moves, you fix one row and miss the other.
Insert: you can't record a new customer until they order.
Delete: removing Ben's only order also loses his town.

cards.title: The first three forms
bullets: 1NF: each cell holds a single value (no 'pen,ink' lists), and a key identifies each row.
2NF: 1NF, and every non-key column depends on the whole key, not part of a two-column key.
3NF: 2NF, and no non-key column depends on another non-key column.

cards.title: The fix and trade-off
cards.body: Split the example into customers(id, name, town) and orders(id, customer_id, item). Now the town lives in one row. The price is more joins when you read; some systems copy data back on purpose (denormalize) to make reads faster.
